# Topic at a Glance

> **One-sentence summary:** A suffix tree or suffix array stores all suffixes of a reference in lexicographic order, making a query sequence's shared prefix with those suffixes directly searchable.

| Item | Description |
|---|---|
| **Biological question** | Where does an exact read, motif, or subsequence occur in a reference or database sequence? |
| **Computational problem** | Index a fixed text so exact substrings can be found without scanning every position |
| **Method type** | Full-text string index |
| **Typical input** | A terminated DNA, RNA, or protein reference and a query pattern |
| **Typical output** | A match interval, count, or reference coordinates |
| **Prerequisites** | Lexicographic order and [k-mers and sequence composition](k-mers-and-sequence-composition.qmd) |
| **Related topics** | [Burrows--Wheeler transform](burrows-wheeler-transform.qmd), [FM-index for sequence search](fm-index-for-sequence-search.qmd), hash indexes |

# The central representation

For a terminated text $T$ of length $n$, suffix $i$ is $T[i..n-1]$. A **suffix tree** is a rooted, edge-labelled trie in which every suffix ends at a leaf; path compression collapses non-branching paths. A **suffix array** is the simpler array $SA$ of suffix start positions sorted by the suffix strings:

$$
T[SA[0]..] < T[SA[1]..] < \cdots < T[SA[n-1]..].
$$

Both representations expose the same fact: all suffixes beginning with a query $P$ occur together in lexicographic order. In a tree, follow the characters of $P$ from the root. In an array, binary-search for the first and last suffix with prefix $P$. The resulting interval contains every exact occurrence; its width is the match count.

## A small example

For `GATAGACA$`, sorted suffixes begin:

```text
8  $
7  A$
3  AGACA$
5  ACA$
1  ATAGACA$
6  CA$
0  GATAGACA$
4  GACA$
2  TAGACA$
```

The suffixes beginning with `GA` are `GATAGACA$` and `GACA$`; they are adjacent in the suffix array. Thus `GA` occurs at positions 0 and 4. A suffix tree reaches the same two leaves by following the path labelled `G` then `A`.

# Construction and auxiliary information

Naively comparing all suffix strings is expensive. Linear-time suffix-tree algorithms, notably Ukkonen's online construction, maintain active suffixes and suffix links while processing the text. Modern suffix-array construction algorithms avoid storing all suffix strings explicitly and often use prefix-doubling, induced sorting, or specialized external-memory methods.

Suffix arrays are commonly paired with a longest-common-prefix (LCP) array, where `LCP[i]` is the shared-prefix length of adjacent suffixes `SA[i-1]` and `SA[i]`. LCP values make repeated-substring and maximal-match calculations efficient. They also show why suffix arrays are useful for genome comparison, not only exact lookup: shared prefixes summarize repeated sequence context.

| Representation | Strength | Cost or limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Suffix tree | Pattern traversal and some interval operations are direct | Pointer-rich representation can use substantial memory |
| Suffix array + LCP | Compact contiguous arrays; binary search is simple | Coordinate lookup and richer queries may need auxiliary structures |
| [FM-index](fm-index-for-sequence-search.qmd) | Compresses suffix order via BWT and supports backward search | Requires rank data structures and sampled suffix-array values for locating |

# Bioinformatics uses and limits

Generalized suffix trees or arrays concatenate several sequences using distinct separators. They can identify exact shared substrings, maximal repeats, or candidate anchors between genomes. A production reference must include separators that prevent a match from crossing contig boundaries.

These indexes answer **exact** substring questions. A sequencing error, allele, or indel can break a query's path or make its interval empty. Approximate matching needs backtracking, dynamic programming, or seed-and-extend logic. For fixed genomic references, compressed suffix-order indexes are widely used in mappers; for sparse candidate generation, [minimizers and sequence sketching](minimizers-and-sequence-sketching.qmd) trade exhaustive indexing for fewer sampled seeds.

Repetitive genomes add an interpretive limitation: a nonempty interval can contain many valid coordinates. The index correctly reports multiplicity but does not decide which locus produced a read. Alignment scoring and mapping-quality models are needed downstream.

# Connections

Suffix arrays are the ordered backbone behind the [Burrows--Wheeler transform](burrows-wheeler-transform.qmd): reading the character preceding each suffix in suffix-array order produces the BWT (with careful sentinel handling). The [FM-index](fm-index-for-sequence-search.qmd) then retains the ability to search suffix intervals while using compressed rank queries. In contrast, [BLAST seed-and-extend search](blast-seed-and-extend-search.qmd) uses short words to avoid a full exact index of every suffix and spends alignment effort only near candidate hits.

# Take-home Messages

1. Suffix trees and suffix arrays organize every suffix of a sequence by lexicographic order.
2. Exact matches of a pattern form one contiguous suffix-array interval or one suffix-tree subtree.
3. LCP information supports repeat and shared-substring analyses in addition to lookup.
4. The indexes do not by themselves solve approximate alignment or ambiguity in repetitive regions.
